# Inclusive Mentoring and Mentee Development {#sec-mentoring}

Mentoring is not a side activity at RIPLRT — it is part of the mission. **Inclusive workforce development** is the final link in our scientific through-line, and mentee co-authorship and growth are documented evidence that we deliver on it. This chapter is our mentoring compact.

## What inclusive mentoring means here

Inclusive mentoring means we mentor for **the mentee's trajectory**, not only for the project's output; we recruit and support members with attention to who has historically been excluded from STEM; and we make sure inclusion shows up in our *practices*, not just our branding.

We recruit and develop members for more than grades or technical skill. We look for and cultivate **curiosity, reliability, kindness, willingness to collaborate, a growth mindset, and independent thinking.** GPA alone has never built a good scientist.

## The Mentoring Skills Model

We treat mentoring as a **set of learnable skills**, not a personality trait — some shared by everyone in a mentoring relationship, some specific to each side of it. We adapt this from the **Mentoring Skills Model** (Linda Phillips-Jones, PhD), which sorts the skills into three regions.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-mentoring-skills
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-cap: "The Mentoring Skills Model — shared core skills practiced by both sides, plus mentee- and mentor-specific skills (adapted from the Mentoring Skills Model, Linda Phillips-Jones, PhD)."
flowchart LR
    MENTEE["<b>Mentee-Specific Skills</b><br/>Acquiring mentors<br/>Learning quickly<br/>Showing initiative<br/>Following through<br/>Managing the relationship"]
    SHARED["<b>Shared Core Skills</b><br/>Listening actively<br/>Building trust<br/>Encouraging<br/>Identifying goals and current reality"]
    MENTOR["<b>Mentor-Specific Skills</b><br/>Instructing / developing capabilities<br/>Inspiring<br/>Providing corrective feedback<br/>Managing risks<br/>Opening doors"]

    MENTEE --- SHARED --- MENTOR

    classDef core stroke-width:2px;
    class SHARED core;
```
Source: [https://my.lerner.udel.edu/wp-content/uploads/Skills_for_Sucessful_Mentoring.pdf](https://my.lerner.udel.edu/wp-content/uploads/Skills_for_Sucessful_Mentoring.pdf)

As @fig-mentoring-skills shows, the three regions map directly onto how our group works:

- **Shared core skills** — *listening actively, building trust, encouraging,* and *identifying goals and current reality* — are the foundation we expect from **everyone, in every direction**: PI to trainee, peer to peer, alumni fellow to current student, and collaborator to collaborator.
- **Mentee-specific skills** — *acquiring mentors, learning quickly, showing initiative, following through,* and *managing the relationship* — are what we actively coach trainees to build. They map onto the development ladder later in this chapter and onto your IDP.
- **Mentor-specific skills** — *instructing and developing capabilities, inspiring, providing corrective feedback, managing risks,* and *opening doors* — are what mentors grow into. In our group these are **not the PI's job alone**: senior mentees, Graduate Research Alumni Fellows, Postdoctoral Collaborating Mentees and Fellows, and Faculty Collaborators all carry mentor-specific responsibilities (@sec-roles-pods).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Use the model in your IDP
At each IDP check-in, name **one shared-core skill, one role-specific skill,** and one concrete way you will practice each this term. Mentors do the same for their mentor-specific skills. Mentoring is a practice we improve on purpose — not something we assume we already have.
:::

Because the group is built around **Inclusive Workforce Development**, most members sit on **both sides of this model at once**: a graduate student is a mentee to the PI and a mentor to an undergraduate; a postdoctoral fellow both receives and provides mentorship. The model is a shared language for getting better at both roles — not a hierarchy.

## The mentoring compact

**Mentors commit to:**

- Meet regularly with mentees (see cadence below) and come prepared.
- Co-create an **Individual Development Plan (IDP)** and revisit it each semester.
- Give honest, kind, timely feedback — and receive it too.
- Map every mentee to a real, credited deliverable.
- Be the first line of support for helping mentees understand and follow this manual.
- Advocate for mentees' growth, visibility, and next steps.
- Practice cultural humility and make space for mentees to bring their whole selves.

**Mentees commit to:**

- Take ownership of their development and the IDP.
- Communicate early about obstacles, confusion, or capacity.
- Learn in public — ask questions, surface mistakes, and try.
- Help mentor those who come after them.
- Follow integrity, data-governance, and authorship rules without exception.

## Meeting cadence

| Touchpoint | Frequency | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| One-on-one mentoring meeting | Biweekly (min. monthly) | [**One-on-One Meeting Template**](/templates/pdf/one-on-one-meeting.pdf) |
| IDP review | Each semester | [**Individual Development Plan Template**](/templates/pdf/individual-development-plan.pdf) |
| Pod check-in | Weekly | [**Weekly Meeting Agenda Template**](/templates/pdf/weekly-meeting-agenda.pdf) |
| Climate / belonging pulse | Quarterly | @sec-annual-review |

## The student-development pathway

Mentees grow along a deliberate ladder. The goal is increasing **independence and leadership**, not just task volume.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Onboard<br/>learn tools, ethics,<br/>one defined task] --> B[Contribute<br/>own a deliverable:<br/>figure, codebook,<br/>lit-synthesis]
    B --> C[Lead a component<br/>analysis, writing,<br/>dashboard within a pod]
    C --> D[Co-author & present<br/>abstract, poster,<br/>manuscript section]
    D --> E[Mentor & lead<br/>project lead, mentor<br/>junior members]
```

### Training milestones

- **Foundation:** complete CITI/IRB training as applicable; learn the group's tools (Git/GitHub, R or Python, the data-governance rules); read this manual.
- **Contribution:** independently own a named deliverable (a figure, a codebook, a literature synthesis, a reproducible notebook).
- **Leadership:** lead a pod component; mentor a newer member; first- or co-first-author a scholarly product.

## Mentee co-authorship as mission evidence

We deliberately document trainee co-authorship across abstracts, posters, presentations, and manuscripts. This does **double duty**: it is genuine scientific output *and* it is proof of our workforce-development mission — useful in IDPs, grant mentoring plans, training-grant applications, and program reviews. Authorship is governed by the rules in @sec-authorship; mentees are credited fairly and, where appropriate, on a **student-first authorship pathway.**

## Tiered, scalable mentoring

No single person can one-on-one mentor a portfolio this large. We use the **tiered pod structure** (@sec-roles-pods): senior mentees mentor junior mentees under PI oversight. This both protects bandwidth and gives senior mentees real leadership training. Mentoring others is itself a development milestone.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Mentoring is reciprocal and developmental
Good mentoring is not the senior person doing the junior person's thinking. It is structured support that transfers capability. When in doubt, ask: "Did this interaction make my mentee *more* able to do this independently next time?"
:::

## Sponsorship vs. mentorship

Mentoring helps people grow; **sponsorship** uses your standing to open doors for them — nominating them for awards, recommending them for opportunities, putting their name forward when they're not in the room. RIPLRT mentors are expected to *sponsor*, not just *mentor*, as members become ready. Track sponsorship moments in the IDP so they don't get lost.
